name: Andrew Johnson
role: President of the United States (1865-1869); earlier Tennessee legislator, congressman, governor and senator
summary: Andrew Johnson was a Jacksonian Democrat who championed small farmers and homesteads against planter and corporate privilege, held that secession was unlawful, and defended the executive and the states' rights against Congress. After the war he opposed military rule over the South and Black suffrage imposed by Congress, favouring white-controlled state governments.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: In his July 1864 letter accepting the vice-presidential nomination he called slavery 'the real cause of the rebellion' and said it and the rebellion must go down together.

revolution-justified.rationale: In his December 1860 Senate speech he said that a people whose grievances are without remedy and whose oppression is intolerable have 'the inherent right of revolution', while denying that secession met that test.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In his July 1861 Senate speech he defended suspending habeas corpus and imposing martial law during the rebellion, citing Jackson at New Orleans, and as military governor of Tennessee he held critics without trial; in peacetime he opposed the same powers.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: His 1867 veto condemns government by military officers who could punish without trial and says free peoples have always struggled to hold rulers within the law, since unrestrained authority cannot safely be trusted; he draws the line between war and peacetime, so his wartime rule in Tennessee is not treated as contrary.

consent-of-governed.rationale: His vetoes argue that Congress should respect the will of a community's inhabitants and that sovereign power lies in the body of the people, and he objected to forcing laws on states 'which they are unwilling to accept'; he applied this to white voters and not to freedmen.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In 1848 he attacked the judiciary's final veto over Congress as unaccountable to the people, but in 1867 he invoked constitutional limits, jury trial and habeas corpus against a congressional majority, so the evidence points both ways.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: His 1848 speech describes the hereditary British king as not responsible to the people and using the veto against popular will, and treats the union of veto and royalty as the end of the people's tribunes.

elective-rulers.rationale: He told the House in 1848 that an officer chosen by the people is their 'tribune' and the safe holder of power, contrasted with a hereditary king, and as a congressman he repeatedly proposed amending the Constitution so the people vote directly for President.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: In his 1858 Homestead speech he warned that land monopoly and a 'bloated, corrupted aristocracy' on one side and dependants on the other destroyed Rome, and said the middle class should keep control of government.

corporate-influence.rationale: In his Homestead speech he complained that nearly all legislation is for 'corporations, monopolies, classes, and individuals' while the producing majority is neglected, citing millions of acres granted to railroad corporations.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: His December 1867 message says enormous frauds have been committed on the Treasury and colossal fortunes made at public expense; as a congressman he attacked clerks and officials as idle and sought pay cuts.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: His 1868 message asks that taxes fall most heavily on luxuries and leave the necessaries of life as free of tax as possible, and as a congressman he opposed the tariff on tea and sugar.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Moore's 1866 biography reports that, believing the rich should bear the burdens of government, he moved an amendment to the tariff bill taxing capital instead of labor, and as military governor he levied heavy taxes on planters and large landholders.

homestead-ownership.rationale: His Homestead bill gave free title to settlers who lived on and cultivated public land, but through a grant of the public domain by Congress rather than a right arising from first claim alone.

ban-cartels.rationale: His 1865 message says monopolies 'ought never to be granted' and must yield to the government, and urges Congress to stop selfish impediments such as monopolies of transit.

reduce-immigration.rationale: His messages welcome immigrants: ending slavery would draw free labor from 'all parts of the civilized world', the homestead policy 'invites emigration from the Old World', and he cites the throngs of emigrants as a sign of confidence in the country.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: His 1865 message says the country's size and variety protect it against every temptation to 'entangling alliances' and that his aim is peace and amity with all nations.

non-intervention.rationale: His 1867 message calls nonintervention a 'sacred principle' as important to every commercial nation as to the United States, and his Mexico policy pressed France to withdraw and adopt the nonintervention attitude the United States held.

death-penalty.rationale: In 1865 he said death is 'too easy' a punishment for conscious leaders of treason, that the assassin of the President should pay with his life, and that 'mercy without justice is a crime'.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: His 1867 veto holds that the federal government has no power to regulate a state's suffrage and that victory over rebels did not subject states to Congress's arbitrary rule; he insisted states keep their rights under the Constitution.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Varon reports he opposed federal funding of internal improvements, yet his messages back the Pacific Railroad as a national object and grant lands to the corporations building it, so the evidence is mixed.

notes:
Independent second pass. Searched his own speeches in Moore's 1866 collection (veto power, Homestead, secession, war, 1864-65 addresses), the vetoes of the Reconstruction acts and the District of Columbia suffrage bill, and the annual messages, by theme. Themes with little or no recorded view: society, culture, ecology and technology. Where a theme rests on wartime acts (habeas corpus, military governorship), they are recorded as his own words and record, not a government's.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 31 answers taken from it, 1 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: No inferred answers. Four complete annual messages, civil-rights and relief vetoes and the full constitutional-reform proposal were downloaded and searched across themes. The whole 490-statement list and remaining unknowns were reviewed. Earlier proslavery identification is not treated as his mature support for continued slavery: he helped abolish it, while rejecting racial political equality. Claims of universal natural rights are retained alongside his contrary racial positions at low confidence. Wartime suppression and later attacks on military Reconstruction are distinguished, rather than assuming either an unconditional libertarian or an unconditional repression position. Judicial term limits are not conflated with recallable judges. A single presidential term does not establish term limits for every office. Specie redemption does not imply abolition of central banking, and criticism of interest and bank privilege does not imply banning all interest. Peaceful expansion is supported by his own 1868 advocacy, not merely assent to Seward’s Alaska purchase. Neither general racial prejudice nor claims of governmental incapacity establish genetic causation. Reservations establish relocation policy, not authority of tribes over every traditional territory. Consent for a proposed island purchase does not address disputed-territory plebiscites. A promise to honor treaty rights does not by itself establish the specific rule that alteration always requires both parties’ agreement. No modern climate, technology, sexual-law or women’s-suffrage position assigned without evidence. The 1875 return to the Senate was reviewed for chronology; no later repudiation of these substantive positions was found.
